prompt.context: Our client, Dark Sky, is a small manufacturer of unmanned (i.e. remotely piloted) data collection aircraft. Dark Sky produces the Assessor, an aircraft originally designed for unmanned weather exploration. In 2003, the United States military began purchasing Assessors for use in Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) missions. The Assessor is profitable, but sales have stagnated and the client wishes to grow.
prompt.question: What are some steps Dark Sky could take to achieve growth?

clarifying_info.q: What does the aircraft do / how does it work?
clarifying_info.a: Dark Sky designs a unique aircraft that is launched from a catapult device; it can be launched from ships at sea or from harsh terrain such as desert or mountains.

clarifying_info.q: Does Dark Sky sell any other products?
clarifying_info.a: Dark Sky only sells the Assessor, but has designed prototypes specifically for military operations.

clarifying_info.q: What is the capacity situation / can Dark Sky scale?
clarifying_info.a: The firm has additional capacity and is positioned to strengthen any division of the workforce if required, including sales force, manufacturing, and R&D.

There are approximately 20 competitors that manufacture unmanned aircraft. Though too small to purchase a competitor, Dark Sky has been considered an acquisition target. Dark Sky's lack of growth in recent years concerns potential buyers.

clarifying_info.q: Who are Dark Sky's customers and what is the pricing structure?
clarifying_info.a: Dark Sky's only customer is the U.S. Military. Dark Sky has a Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee contract with the U.S. Military for Assessor sales. The contract has been extended in the past and is up for renegotiation; the Military has agreed to a marginal price increase to account for inflation. Contracts for new aircraft will be structured similarly.

exhibits.title: Dark Sky Revenue 2000–2010
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing Dark Sky annual revenue in millions of dollars from approximately 2000 to 2010
exhibits.data: Revenue axis from 0 to 5 ($, Million); years shown: 2000, 2002, 2004, 2006, 2008, 2010; bars indicate revenue grew from near zero around 2000–2001, rose steeply through 2002–2006, and then leveled off near $5M through 2010

exhibits.title: New Product Sales Forecast, 2011
exhibits.shows: A table comparing three new aircraft prototypes across Navy units sold, Army units sold, Assessor cannibalization rate, and price per aircraft; also lists updated Assessor price
exhibits.data: SeaBird: Navy 50, Army 0, Assessor cannibalization 40%, price $220,000 | SandBird: Navy 0, Army 60, Assessor cannibalization 70%, price $210,000 | JointBird: Navy 38, Army 52, Assessor cannibalization 90%, price $180,000 | Assessor price: $110,000

framework: • Increase penetration: negotiate additional Assessor sales to the military
• Product development: develop new aircraft or add-ons that appeal to the military
• New market entry: sell the Assessor to international markets or domestic non-military buyers (e.g. Border Patrol, police, news channels)
• Diversification: develop a new product for a new market
• Pricing: leverage contract renegotiation to increase price (already agreed to 10% increase)
• Joint venture: partner with a firm to expand market access or develop a product beyond Dark Sky's current capability
• M&A: acquire a firm to add capacity and/or product mix; alternatively position Dark Sky as an attractive acquisition target by demonstrating growth

questions.prompt: Exhibit 1a: How many units were sold in 2010?
questions.guidance: Read revenue from chart (~$5M), divide by unit price ($100K). Strong candidates do this quickly as a warm-up calculation.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 1b: What was the revenue growth rate from 2002 to 2006?
questions.guidance: Read 2002 revenue (~$500K) and 2006 revenue (~$5,000K) from chart, apply percentage change formula.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2: To maximize short-term (2011) revenue, which new aircraft should Dark Sky introduce?
questions.guidance: Calculate total 2011 revenue for each scenario: Assessor revenue (with post-price-increase $110K price, adjusted for cannibalization) plus new product revenue. Compare all four options including Assessor-only baseline. Candidate should organize calculation systematically and use mental math shortcuts.

math.setup: Assessor baseline: 50 units at $110,000 each = $5,500,000. Each new product reduces Assessor units by its cannibalization rate. New product units and prices from Exhibit 2.
math.answer: JointBird yields the highest total revenue at $16,750,000

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways Dark Sky could achieve organic or inorganic growth?

categories.name: Organic – Market Penetration
ideas: Negotiate additional Assessor unit sales to the military
Expand Assessor use to new military branches or commands

categories.name: Organic – Product Development
ideas: Develop new unmanned aircraft prototypes (SeaBird, SandBird, JointBird)
Add training services for military personnel operating aircraft
Develop aircraft accessories or add-on sensor packages

categories.name: Organic – New Market Entry
ideas: Sell the Assessor to international militaries or allied governments
Sell to domestic non-military customers: Border Patrol, local police, news channels
Explore civilian scientific or environmental monitoring markets

categories.name: Organic – Diversification
ideas: Develop a new unmanned product (e.g. ground-based drone) for a different customer segment
License the catapult-launch technology to other manufacturers

categories.name: Organic – Pricing
ideas: Leverage contract renegotiation to achieve price increases beyond inflation
Introduce premium pricing tiers for enhanced sensor/capability configurations

categories.name: External – Joint Venture
ideas: Partner with a larger defense contractor to gain access to new military contracts
Contract with a technology firm to co-develop advanced sensor payloads

categories.name: External – M&A
ideas: Acquire a smaller competitor to add product mix or production capacity
Position Dark Sky as an attractive acquisition target to a larger defense firm by demonstrating growth trajectory

recommendation: Dark Sky should introduce the JointBird to the U.S. Military in 2011 to maximize short-term revenue; the JointBird scenario yields $16,750,000 in total revenue versus $5,500,000 for the Assessor-only baseline
The JointBird's dual Army/Navy applicability (90 combined units) offsets its lower unit price and heavy Assessor cannibalization, making it the highest-revenue option among the three new aircraft
risks: Heavy Assessor cannibalization (90%) reduces the long-term Assessor revenue stream and customer relationship
Profitability of each aircraft under the Cost-Plus contract is likely similar per unit, but total cost to set up manufacturing for JointBird must be evaluated
Competitive response: 20 competitors in the market may offer similar joint-service aircraft at lower prices
Dependence on a single customer (U.S. Military) creates significant contract renewal risk
next_steps: Assess how quickly Dark Sky can begin manufacturing JointBird and whether a phased approach (add SandBird or SeaBird in year two) could further increase multi-year revenues
Evaluate the payback period and capital investment required for each new aircraft manufacturing line
Analyze whether the residual $550,000 Assessor revenue under the JointBird scenario justifies maintaining Assessor production, or whether those resources should be redeployed
Explore medium-term growth via new market entry (e.g. Border Patrol, international sales) to reduce dependence on U.S. Military contracts
